The long gallery was dim and forbidding, as if the sun had not reached it in years. At the far end stood a wide door, and on the door a golden ring shone bright. They pushed it open, and there was the Great King of the Golden Roc.

The Great King of the Golden Roc was not a big man. The years, and the wearing-away of his great ambitions, seemed to have shrunk and withered him, as a splendid cockscomb withers in a vexing west wind. He sat in a broad mandarin's chair heaped with brocade cushions, so that he looked, all told, like a withered pine sunk in a bank of mountain cloud.
Yet Lu Xiaofeng was not disappointed, for there was still a light in the old man's eyes, and about him still an air of dignity and nobility beyond words.
The broad-eared, long-legged hound had got back before them, and lay now curled at his feet.
Princess Danfeng crossed softly to him and knelt at his feet, seeming to tell over in a low voice how their errand had gone.
But the Great King's bright eyes stayed fixed on Lu Xiaofeng all the while. "Young man," he said suddenly, "come here."
His voice was low and strong, and what he said had the ring of a command. Lu Xiaofeng did not come.
Lu Xiaofeng was not a man used to taking orders. Instead he sat down, well across the room, in a chair facing the old man.
The room was dim, but the Great King's eyes only shone the brighter. "You are Lu Xiaofeng?" he said sharply.
"Lu Xiaofeng," said he lightly, "not Shangguan Danfeng."
For he knew by now that the King too was a Shangguan. In that old royal house every one of them had borne the surname Shangguan, and gloried in it, generation upon generation.
The Great King laughed aloud. "Good. Lu Xiaofeng is Lu Xiaofeng indeed. It seems we've not sought out the wrong man."
"And I hope I've not come to the wrong man either," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You've come for Hua Manlou?" said the Great King.
Lu Xiaofeng nodded.
"He is well," said the Great King. "Grant me one thing, and you may see him whenever you like."
"And what thing is that?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
The Great King did not answer him directly.

He gazed at a ring of curious make upon his finger, and a strange radiance kindled all at once in his aged face. A long while passed before he spoke, slowly. "Ours is a very old kingdom. It stood already, long before this dynasty of yours was ever founded."
His voice gathered strength; plainly he took pride in his name and his blood.
Lu Xiaofeng had no wish to spoil an old man's dignity in his last years, and so he only listened, and said nothing.
"Our kingdom is fallen now," said the Great King, "but the blood in our veins is royal blood still. While one of our line remains alive, the kingdom can never be destroyed."
His voice was full not only of pride, but of certainty.
It struck Lu Xiaofeng that there was, after all, something in the old man worth respecting: here, at the least, was no man easily brought down.
Lu Xiaofeng had always respected such men, respected their courage and their faith.

"Our kingdom was founded in a far country," the Great King went on, "but age after age it lived in ease and plenty. The fields gave rich harvests, and in the deep mountains lay gold-sand and treasure beyond counting."
Lu Xiaofeng could not help asking, "Then why did you come to the Central Lands?"

The radiance died from the Great King's face, and into his eyes came a look of deep pain and hatred. "It was our very wealth that woke the greed of a neighbouring state. They made a league with the mailed horsemen of the Cossacks, and led an army against us."

He went on, sombre now. "That was fifty years ago. I was still a child. The old King had ever been a ruler of peace and letters, and could not stand against so fierce and savage a cavalry; yet he resolved to hold to the death, and perish with his land."
"And it was he who sent you to take refuge in the Central Lands?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

The Great King nodded. "To preserve some part of our strength, and work one day for a restoration, he not only insisted that I go, he divided the treasury into four shares and gave them into the hands of four trusted ministers, charging them to bring me into the Central Lands."

A look of gratitude crossed his face. "One of the four was my uncle, Shangguan Jin. He brought me here, and with the share he carried he bought land and houses, so that our household has lived free of care to this day. His kindness to us I shall never, while I live, forget."
"And the other three?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
The Great King's gratitude turned again to fury. "From the day I parted from my father the King, I never saw them again. But their names, too, I shall never forget."
Lu Xiaofeng had just begun to see the shape of the thing, and asked at once, "What are they called?"
The Great King clenched both fists. "Shangguan Mu," he said with hatred. "Ping Duhe. Yan Liben."
Lu Xiaofeng considered. "I've never heard of any of the three."
"But the men themselves you will certainly have seen."
"Oh?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The moment they reached the Central Lands, they changed their names and surnames. Only a year ago did I trace where they had gone."
He made a sudden sign to his daughter, and Princess Danfeng took from a stout old cabinet behind his seat three scroll-albums.
"Painted here," said the Great King bitterly, "are the three of them. Two at least, I think, you'll know."
Each scroll bore two portraits, one young, one aged; the two being one and the same man.
Princess Danfeng spread open the first scroll. "The upper likeness is how he looked when he left the palace. The lower is how we found him a year ago, as he is now."
This man had a round face, all smiles, and a kindly look, but for a great hooked nose like an eagle's beak.
Lu Xiaofeng frowned. "This looks very like Yan Tieshan, of the Yan jewel-house of Guanzhong."
The Great King set his teeth. "Just so. Yan Tieshan today is the Yan Liben of those years. I thank Heaven only that it has not yet let him die."
The man in the second painting had high cheekbones and a pair of three-cornered eyes that flashed with authority, a man of great power, one saw at a glance.
At the sight of him, Lu Xiaofeng's face changed.
"This is Ping Duhe," said the Great King. "His name now is Dugu Yihe, and the head of the Blue-Robe Tower is none other than he."
Lu Xiaofeng started, and was a long time silent before he said slowly, "I know this man too. But I never knew he was the master of the First Tower of the Blue-Robe."
He let out a long sigh. "I knew him only as the present master of the Emei sword-sect."

The Great King said with hatred, "He has hidden himself well. No one in the world, I dare say, would ever dream that the upright and honourable master of Emei is the traitor who sold his own country and his old lord."
The third likeness was of a lean little old man: small, solitary, clean, and tough.
Lu Xiaofeng nearly cried out. "Huo Xiu!"
"Just so. Huo Xiu. The name Shangguan Mu goes by now is Huo Xiu."

He went on. "They call Huo Xiu the most fabled of men: how, fifty years ago, he came out into the world barehanded and empty, and of a sudden, as by a miracle, became the richest man under heaven. To this day, save for you, there is likely not a soul in the jianghu who knows how that vast fortune was got."
Lu Xiaofeng's face went pale. He drew back a few slow steps and sat down in a chair.
The Great King watched him. "By now, I think, you can guess what it is we ask of you."
Lu Xiaofeng was long silent, then sighed. "And yet I still don't know what it is you truly want."
The Great King clenched his fists and beat them on the arms of his chair. "I want nothing," he said fiercely. "Nothing but justice."
"And justice means revenge?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
The Great King's face went iron-grey, and he said nothing.
"Is it revenge you want me to take for you?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Again the Great King was long silent, then let out a heavy sigh. "They are old men now, all of them, with one foot in the coffin. And I am old too. Do you suppose I still wish to kill them?"
He shook his own head, denying his own words. "But no more can I let them go scot-free."
Lu Xiaofeng said nothing. There was nothing he could say.
"First," said the Great King sharply, "I will have them return the treasure they carried out of the Golden Roc to the Golden Roc, to be the foundation of its restoration in days to come."
It was a just demand, that.
"Second, I will have them go in person before the spirit-tablet of the old King, and there repent their sins, that his soul in Heaven may find some little comfort."
Lu Xiaofeng thought a while, and sighed. "Both demands are just enough, it's true."
The Great King's face cleared. "I knew you for an upright and fair-minded young man, one who would never refuse such a thing."
Lu Xiaofeng thought again for a long while, and smiled ruefully. "My fear is that both will be very hard to bring about."
"If even you cannot," said the Great King, "who can?"
"Perhaps no one can," said Lu Xiaofeng.

He went on quickly. "These three men are now among the most illustrious in the land. To do as you ask would be as good as confessing the crimes of those years. Their names, their standing, their wealth, all of it would be undone in a single day."
The Great King's face grew darker still. "I know well enough they'll never own to it of their own accord."
"And more," said Lu Xiaofeng. "Their money and their power are grown fearfully great, and each of them commands a martial skill no man can fathom."
"The old King laid this charge on them," said the Great King, "for the very reason that they were among the first masters of the Golden Roc."
"And in these fifty years," said Lu Xiaofeng, "they'll have been guarding at every hour against your coming for revenge. So who knows how far their skill has advanced since?"
He sighed again. "I've often said that in all the world today there are but five or six who have truly reached the summit of the martial arts. Huo Xiu and Dugu Yihe are both among them."
Women are curious after all, and Princess Danfeng could not help asking, "And who are the other three or four?"

"The Shaolin abbot, the Chan master Dabei," said Lu Xiaofeng, "the Wudang elder, the Wooden Taoist. Both have carried the inner and outer arts to their last perfection. But for a sword keen and subtle beyond all others, you must look to the Lord of White Cloud City, Ye Gucheng, of Flying-Immortal Isle in the Southern Sea, and to Ximen Chuixue of the Ten Thousand Plum Manor."
Princess Danfeng gazed at him. "And you yourself?"
Lu Xiaofeng smiled, and said nothing. There was no need.
The Great King sighed once more, heavily. "I know the hardness and the danger of it, and I'll not force you to help us. Take your time, and think it over."
His brow was full of grief and rage. He clenched his fists. "But come what may, we mean to have it out with them ourselves. While one of us is left alive, we'll fight them to the end."
"I understand," said Lu Xiaofeng.
The Great King was silent a long while, then forced a smile and said loudly, "Whatever comes of it, the young lord Lu is our honoured guest. Why is the wine not yet brought?"
Princess Danfeng bowed her head. "I'll have it made ready at once."
"The best of the Persian grape-wine," said the Great King. "And have the young lord Hua brought in as well."
"Yes," said Princess Danfeng.

The Great King looked at Lu Xiaofeng, and his face turned proud and grave again. "Whatever comes," he said slowly, "you are our friend now. The heirs of the Golden Roc have never yet used any man's need to force a friend's hand."
The silver goblets were old and elegant, and the wine within was a pale violet.
Lu Xiaofeng watched in silence as Princess Danfeng poured the wine into the tall, plain cups. Hua Manlou sat at his side.
The two of them said nothing, only gripped each other's hand, hard.
That said everything there was to say. The wine was poured, only three cups.
The Great King looked up and smiled. "For years now I've not been able to drink. Today I'll break my rule and take a cup with the two of you."
But Princess Danfeng shook her head. "I'll drink in your place. Don't forget your legs."
The Great King's eyes flashed, but in the end he smiled ruefully. "Very well, I won't drink. Happily, watching others drink is a pleasure of its own; good wine always lends a man spirit and life."

Princess Danfeng smiled and explained to Lu Xiaofeng, "My father has only to take a mouthful of wine and both his legs swell up at once, till he cannot walk a step. I'm sure the two of you will forgive him."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled and raised his cup.
Princess Danfeng turned, with her back to her father, and made a strange face at Lu Xiaofeng all at once. He could not read it.
Princess Danfeng too raised her cup, smiling. "This is a Persian grape-wine my father has kept cellared for many years. I hope it will suit the two of you."
She lifted her own cup first and drank it down, then sighed lightly. "Good wine indeed."
It is a rare host who praises his own wine over and over, and Princess Danfeng was by no means a woman given to showing herself off.
Lu Xiaofeng was still wondering at it when he realized that what he had drunk was no wine at all, only sugar-water with a little colour added.
All at once he understood what Princess Danfeng had meant, and feared that Hua Manlou, who could not see her face, would miss it.
But Hua Manlou was smiling, and smiling he drank his wine down, and sighed as well. "Good wine indeed!"
Lu Xiaofeng laughed. "I don't think I've ever drunk wine half so good."
The Great King laughed aloud, the first truly happy laugh of the day. "It is a wine hard to come by in this world. But you two young men are worthy of a wine like mine."
Lu Xiaofeng quickly drank three cups more, then said with a smile, "Wine as good as this can't be drunk for nothing, of course."
The Great King's eyes lit, and he looked at him. "You mean to say—"
Lu Xiaofeng drew a long breath. "The justice you want, I'll do my utmost to win back for you."

The Great King rose suddenly to his full height and lurched across to him, gripping his shoulders in both hands. His aged eyes brimmed with hot, grateful tears, and his voice broke. "Thank you, thank you, thank you—"
He said the same two phrases over and over, past all counting.
Princess Danfeng, watching at his side, could not help turning away to wipe her tears in secret.

A long while passed before the Great King grew somewhat calmer. "Dugu Fang and Dugu Yihe are both of the Dugu name, but they hate each other like the deep sea. It was Yan Tieshan who sliced away half of Liu Yuhen's face, and Xiao Qiuyu is Liu Yuhen's sworn brother to the death. Only do this thing for us, and the three of them will go through fire and water at your side."
"They had far better stay here," said Lu Xiaofeng.
The Great King frowned. "Why?"
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "I know well enough they're all first-rank masters of the martial world. But to send them against Dugu Yihe and Huo Xiu would be no better than sending them to their deaths."
"You, you'll want no other helpers, then?" said the Great King.
Lu Xiaofeng patted Hua Manlou lightly on the shoulder, and smiled. "He and I are old partners, after all."
The Great King looked at Hua Manlou, with something like doubt.
He could not really believe this blind man stronger than masters like Liu Yuhen, Xiao Qiuyu, and Dugu Fang; nor, likely, could anyone.
Lu Xiaofeng went on, "Besides him, of course, I'll have to go and find two or three others."
"Find whom?" said the Great King.
Lu Xiaofeng considered. "First I must find Zhu Ting."
"Zhu Ting?" The Great King had plainly never heard the name.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "Zhu Ting is no great fighter, but just now he'll be very useful."
The Great King waited for him to explain.
"Since you've found them," said Lu Xiaofeng, "it may be they've found you as well. When you go to settle accounts with them, they may very well strike first, and kill you to seal your mouth."
The Great King gave a cold laugh. "I'm not afraid."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "You're not afraid; I am. So I must have Zhu Ting here. Only he can turn this place into a fortress no one can easily storm."
"He knows the making of hidden mechanisms and traps?" said the Great King.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "If he sets his hand to it, he can build you a chair that bites."
The Great King laughed too. "It seems you keep a great many strange friends."
"Just now," said Lu Xiaofeng, "my one hope is to talk a certain man into coming out to help me with this."
The Great King's eyes flickered. "He too will be useful?"
"If he'll lend his hand," said Lu Xiaofeng, "the thing has a chance of success. Not otherwise."
"And who is this man?" said the Great King.
"Ximen Chuixue," said Lu Xiaofeng.
The long gallery was darker and more forbidding now. It was afternoon already.
Princess Danfeng walked with her head bowed, her jet-black hair falling to her shoulders like a spring stream. "For what you did just now," she said softly, "I truly don't know how to thank you."
"You mean the cup of wine?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Princess Danfeng coloured, and kept her head down. "You'll have seen by now that my father is a proud man, who can bear no more blows. I've never been willing to let him know the truth."
"I understand," said Lu Xiaofeng.

Princess Danfeng sighed, low and sorrowful. "Save for the sitting-room and bedchamber where the old man passes his days, the rooms of this place stand all but empty. Even the good wine cellared here these many years, we've sold off, jar by jar."

Her head sank lower still. "There is scarcely a soul in our house who can earn a living. To keep it going at all is hard enough, and there is so much else we must do besides. To find you, I even pawned the string of pearls my late mother left me."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "I hadn't rightly understood how things stood with you. But that cup of wine told me a great deal."
Princess Danfeng lifted her head suddenly and gazed at him. "Was it because you'd seen how things stood with us that you agreed?"
"That," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and because he'd taken me for a friend, and used nothing to force my hand."
Princess Danfeng looked at him, and in her lovely eyes there seemed to shine grateful tears.
So she lowered her head quickly, and said softly, "I had you wrong all along. I always thought you a man no feeling could move."
Hua Manlou had been smiling all the while; he listened much and said little. Now he said, still smiling, "I told you. He looks hard and foul, this one, but his heart is soft as bean-curd."
Princess Danfeng could not help a lovely smile. "You're wrong as well, in fact."
"Oh?" said Hua Manlou.
"He may look hard," said Princess Danfeng, "but he isn't the least bit foul."
The words were not out before her own face reddened, and she changed the subject at once. "The guest room is very poor, I'm afraid. I hope the two of you won't mind it."
Lu Xiaofeng gave a little cough. "Perhaps we shouldn't have agreed to stay for supper at all."
Princess Danfeng smiled again. "Don't forget, we still have the four gold ingots you kept back for us."
Lu Xiaofeng's eyes flickered. "So by then you knew old Huo was the man you were seeking?"
"Not until you said it aloud did we know," said Princess Danfeng.
Lu Xiaofeng's face turned suddenly grave. "But how did you know Dugu Yihe was the master of the Blue-Robe Tower? That's one of the deepest secrets in all the jianghu."

Princess Danfeng hesitated, and at last answered. "Because Liu Yuhen was once among his most trusted men. It was for his sake that the gallant Jade-Faced Gentleman of those years became the thing he is today."
Lu Xiaofeng's eyes brightened, as though much had come clear to him all at once.
Princess Danfeng sighed softly. "Love, from of old, leaves only regret behind. He was a grieving man to begin with, and his heart is broken clean through."
The guest room was large, but for a bed, a small table, and a few old chairs there was scarcely any furnishing in it at all.
Hua Manlou sat down. Blind though he was, he always seemed to feel where a chair stood.
Lu Xiaofeng watched him, then asked suddenly, "Have you never once sat down on nothing?"
Hua Manlou smiled. "You'd like me to?"
Lu Xiaofeng laughed too. "I'd only like you to sit down one day and find you'd sat in a woman's lap."
"You've more experience of that than I have," said Hua Manlou.
"If you had as much of it as I do," said Lu Xiaofeng lightly, "perhaps you'd not have been taken in."
"Taken in by whom?" said Hua Manlou.
"Have you forgotten Shangguan Feiyan?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Hua Manlou smiled. "I wasn't taken in. I came of my own will."
Lu Xiaofeng was surprised. "Of your own will? Why?"
"Perhaps because my days of late have been too dull," said Hua Manlou, "and I've had a mind to find myself a dangerous, interesting thing or two to do."
"Or perhaps," said Lu Xiaofeng coldly, "you were simply gulled by a pretty woman who lies very well."
Hua Manlou laughed. "She is a girl who lies very well. But to me she told the truth."
"She'd told you the whole of it beforehand?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Hua Manlou nodded.
"Perhaps she'd found that the best way to handle a man like you is to tell the truth," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Perhaps," said Hua Manlou.
"Her aim was to bring you here," said Lu Xiaofeng. "You came, so her aim was met."
Hua Manlou smiled. "You seem set on making me angry."
"And you're not?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

Hua Manlou laughed. "Why should I be? They fetched me in a carriage and received me as an honoured guest. The weather here is fair, the courtyard full of flowers in bloom. And now you've come too. Even if I really was taken in, I've nothing to complain of."
Lu Xiaofeng could not help laughing. "It seems it's no easy thing to make you angry."
Hua Manlou asked suddenly, "Do you truly mean to go to Ximen Chuixue?"
"Mm," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You think you can talk him into lifting a hand for another man's sake?" said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled ruefully. "I know there seems to be nothing on earth that can move him. But I must at least try."
"And then?" said Hua Manlou.
"I haven't thought further yet," said Lu Xiaofeng. "Only to go about outside for a while, and see what there is to see."
"And what is it you want to see?" said Hua Manlou.
"What I'd most like to see, perhaps," said Lu Xiaofeng, "is Shangguan Feiyan."
Hua Manlou was smiling still, but there was a shade of worry in the smile now. "You won't find her," he said quietly.
"Why not?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Since I came, I've not once heard her voice," said Hua Manlou. "It seems she's left this place."
Lu Xiaofeng looked at him, and something of the same worry seemed to come into his own eyes.
But Hua Manlou smiled again. "She seems a woman who finds it hard to settle anywhere."
Lu Xiaofeng laughed too, all at once. "And what woman isn't, when you come to it?"
The room had just fallen dark. Hua Manlou sat alone in it, quiet, and looked as glad and untroubled as ever.
He was forever glad and content, for wherever he was, he could taste some pleasure that others could not.
Just now he was savouring the dusk of a late-spring evening, in the third month of the year.
Then he heard a knocking at the door.
The knock had scarcely sounded before the door was pushed open and two men came in: Dugu Fang and Xiao Qiuyu.
But there was the tread of only one man. Dugu Fang's step was lighter than the spring wind itself.
Hua Manlou smiled. "Sit, both of you. There are a few chairs still, I know."
He did not ask their errand, nor who they were. Whoever came into his room, he welcomed alike, and would share alike with them all that he had.
But Dugu Fang's face darkened. "How did you know there were two of us?" he said coldly. "Are you truly blind, or not?"
He had believed no one could ever hear his footfall; he had always been proud of his lightness-skill. And so Dugu Fang was displeased now.
But Hua Manlou was as glad as ever, and smiled. "There are times I hardly believe it myself. For to my mind the only truly blind man is the one who has eyes and will not use them to see."
Xiao Qiuyu was smiling too. "You forget there's another kind of man who is truly blind."
"What kind?" said Hua Manlou.
"A dead one," said Xiao Qiuyu.
Hua Manlou laughed. "And how do you know the dead are blind? Perhaps they see a great deal too. None of us has died yet, so how should we know what the dead feel?"
"Perhaps you'll soon find out," said Dugu Fang coldly.
"We don't know you," said Xiao Qiuyu easily, "and we bear you no grudge. But we've come to kill you all the same."
Hua Manlou showed not the least alarm, nor even displeasure. He went on smiling. "As it happens, I've been expecting the two of you for some while."
"You knew we'd come to kill you?" said Dugu Fang.
"Lu Xiaofeng is no fool," said Hua Manlou. "But he's made far more enemies than he imagines, for there are times he talks like a cannon going off."
Dugu Fang gave a cold laugh.

"No man likes to be thought less than a blind one, least of all masters such as the two of you," said Hua Manlou. "It's not to be borne. Of course you'd come to measure yourselves against the blind man." His face was as calm as ever, and he went on slowly. "That is the one thing a hero of the jianghu can never swallow."
"And you?" said Dugu Fang.
"I'm no hero. I'm only a blind man," said Hua Manlou.
Dugu Fang was still smiling coldly, but he could not keep the astonishment from his face.
This blind man knew altogether too much.
"You knew we were coming, and waited here for us?" said Xiao Qiuyu.
"Where should a blind man run to?" said Hua Manlou.
"Die, then!" Dugu Fang cried suddenly.
With the shout he struck, and a bright chain-spear darted like a viper at Hua Manlou's throat.
The Heartbreak Sword was out as well.
Xiao Qiuyu's stroke was slow, and slow it made no wind; a blind man cannot see a sword, and knows it only by the wind of its coming.
But this stroke raised no wind at all. This was the stroke to break a blind man's heart in truth.
And before it came the viper of the chain-spear, pressing the attack. Even should the spear not strike home at a blow, the sword behind it could not miss.
But Xiao Qiuyu had reckoned wrong.
This blind man, besides the hearing of his ears, seemed to have some strange and secret sense as well.
He seemed to feel that the deadly thing was not the spear but the sword, the very stroke he could neither see nor hear.
Before the sword had reached him he twisted aside, and as the chain-spear swept across his shoulder his two hands came together with a clap and caught the blade between them.
Two sharp cracks, and the long sword of tempered steel broke of a sudden into three pieces. It was to have broken a man's heart; instead it was the sword that broke.
The longest piece was still caught in Hua Manlou's hands. He turned his wrist, and the chain-spear was left coiled about the broken blade.
Hua Manlou himself had already slid three zhang across the room, to the window, and come to rest, as it chanced, in a chair beneath it.
Dugu Fang stood stunned, and in the dusk Xiao Qiuyu's face had gone white as a sheet of paper with shock.

Hua Manlou smiled. "I had no wish to offend Master Xiao. But that stroke of yours was a cruel one to use on a blind man. I only hope that when you've found yourself another sword, you'll leave your man a little room to give ground."

The garden had once held flowers and trees in plenty, but many of the branches were broken now. Only now did Lu Xiaofeng understand where the flowers Princess Danfeng had brought with her had come from.
Just then he caught sight of the little girl again.

Shangguan Xue'er stood among the flowers, in the slanting sun. The pale evening light fell on her hair, soft and smooth as silk. She looked as good and biddable as ever, as though she had never told half a lie in her life.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled, and could not help going over to hail her. "Hey there, big cousin."
Shangguan Xue'er glanced back at him and smiled too. "Hey yourself, little cousin."
"Are you well?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I'm not," said Shangguan Xue'er.
"Why not?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I've something on my mind. A great deal on my mind," said Shangguan Xue'er.
Lu Xiaofeng saw of a sudden that her big bright eyes did indeed hold some sadness beyond telling; even her sweet smile seemed to have grown a little forced.
He could not help asking, "What is it that's on your mind?"
"I'm worried about my sister," said Shangguan Xue'er.
"Your sister? Shangguan Feiyan?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Xue'er nodded.
"What is it that worries you?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"She's vanished, all at once," said Shangguan Xue'er.
"When did she vanish?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"The very day Hua Manlou came here," said Shangguan Xue'er. "The same day we went out to find you."
Lu Xiaofeng stared. "If you're worried, why not go out and look for her?"
"Because she said she'd wait here for us to come back," said Shangguan Xue'er.
"And you believe everything she says?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Of course I do," said Shangguan Xue'er.
Lu Xiaofeng could not help a smile. "If she never went out, how could she suddenly be gone?"
"I can't make it out either," said Shangguan Xue'er. "That's why I'm looking for her."
"Looking here, in the garden?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Mm," said Shangguan Xue'er.
"You think she's been hiding in the garden, and for days on end?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"I'm not looking for her," said Shangguan Xue'er. "I'm looking for her body."
Lu Xiaofeng frowned. "Her body?"
"I think someone's killed her, and buried her here in the garden," said Shangguan Xue'er.
"This is your own home," said Lu Xiaofeng. "Who here would kill her?"
"Our home it may be," said Shangguan Xue'er, "but there are others in it."
"What others?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Your friend Hua Manlou, for one," said Shangguan Xue'er.
"You think Hua Manlou would kill?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Why not? Anyone might kill. Even the old King might," said Shangguan Xue'er.
"The old King, kill her? Why?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Just because I don't know why," said Shangguan Xue'er, "that's why I'm looking."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed softly. "You think too much. A little girl of twelve has no business thinking so much."
Shangguan Xue'er looked at him, a long while, before she asked slowly, "And who says I'm only twelve?"
"Your cousin said so," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Her word you believe," said Shangguan Xue'er. "Why not mine?"
"Because—" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Shangguan Xue'er gave a cold little laugh. "Because I've the look of a born liar, is that it?"
Lu Xiaofeng laughed again. "You certainly don't look a woman of twenty."
Shangguan Xue'er looked at him a long while more, then sighed. "Your great failing is that you think yourself too clever. What you should believe, you don't; and what you shouldn't, you do."
The words were not out before her small shape flickered and was gone among the flowers.
The dusk was deepening; even the last stroke of sunset was gone now, and darkness crept slowly over the earth.
The garden full of flowers was losing its colours too, little by little.
Lu Xiaofeng, facing the vague, mist-like dusk, felt all at once that this place had been in a fog from the first. And the people in it too.
The dusk had thickened, and no lamp was lit in the room.
When Lu Xiaofeng came in, Hua Manlou was still sitting at the window, seeming to drink in the spring wind that blew through it, and the scent it carried; everywhere, always, he drank in life itself.
Lu Xiaofeng asked suddenly, "They've been here already?"
"Who has?" said Hua Manlou.
"Dugu Fang and Xiao Qiuyu," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"You knew they'd come?" said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled. "Liu Yuhen would never come to kill you over a thing like this. But those two, they couldn't kill you either."
Hua Manlou gazed at him, and smiled. "You reckoned it very close."
Lu Xiaofeng laughed. "If I hadn't, why would I have slipped out just now?"

"You goaded them into coming on purpose, and slipped out on purpose, to give them their chance at me?" Hua Manlou sighed, and smiled ruefully. "A friend like you is a rare thing to find, and no mistake."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed too, all at once. "That Shangguan Feiyan of yours is a rare thing to find as well."
"You've looked for her?" said Hua Manlou.
"Even her own sister can't find her," said Lu Xiaofeng. "What use would my looking be?"

Across Hua Manlou's calm and peaceful face there passed again a shade of worry. Plainly he had come to feel something out of the common for this girl who had vanished so suddenly, and could not hide it though he tried.
When a feeling like that has entered a man's heart, it is like a pearl among grains of sand: anyone can see it at a glance.
Lu Xiaofeng saw it too, of course, and asked at once, of set purpose, "Have you met the sister?"
"No," said Hua Manlou.
"Then you're in luck, it seems," said Lu Xiaofeng. "Better luck than mine, at any rate."
"The sister's a little handful?" said Hua Manlou.
Lu Xiaofeng smiled ruefully. "A little handful, and worse. A little imp. She can lie a dead man back to life, and she's suspicious into the bargain."
"A suspicious little girl?" said Hua Manlou.
"More suspicious than any old woman," said Lu Xiaofeng. "She even suspects her sister's been murdered, and suspects you and the Great King of the Golden Roc of being the murderers."
He had meant to cheer Hua Manlou, and so he laughed himself.
But there was no sign of cheer in Hua Manlou at all.
Lu Xiaofeng could not help going on, "Isn't that a comical notion of hers?"
"It isn't comical," said Hua Manlou.

"Shangguan Feiyan is only a girl," said Lu Xiaofeng, "who can do little more than tell lies. And what girl of eighteen or nineteen can't tell lies? Why should anyone murder a girl like that, and who could bring himself to so cruel a deed?"
Hua Manlou was silent, and a long while passed before he said slowly, "Just now I have only one hope."
"What hope?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
Hua Manlou smiled. "I only hope the wine they give us tonight is not a false one."
These were not words for Hua Manlou to speak; he was no lover of wine to begin with.
Lu Xiaofeng looked at him, and felt of a sudden that even his smile had turned a little mysterious.
Whoever came to this place, it seemed, turned mysterious at once, and a little strange.
Lu Xiaofeng blinked, and put on a mysterious air of his own, and lowered his voice. "I have a hope as well."
Hua Manlou could not help asking, "What hope?"
"I only hope," said Lu Xiaofeng, "that what they feast us on tonight is not man-flesh buns, and what they pour us not a soul-stealing wine."
